y-m-02-01.title: Are long or tilted cards also quadrilaterals?
y-m-02-01.topic: Plane figures: recognizing the shape of a quadrilateral
y-m-02-01.goal: Find the wrong line in an idea that narrowly takes a quadrilateral to be 'upright with four sides of the same length', set a standard for judging by the number of straight lines and pointed corners, and explain long or tilted quadrilaterals.
y-m-02-01.material: Harin collected three quadrilateral cards. Card 가 sits upright and all four straight lines have the same length. Card 나 is long sideways, so the top and bottom lines are long and the two side lines are short. Card 다 has the same shape as 가 but is tilted so that a pointed corner is at the top. All three cards are surrounded by four straight lines and have four pointed corners. (There is no picture, so picture it in words.) Harin thought like this.
y-m-02-01.thinking.0: Check whether each line of the solution has a reason
y-m-02-01.thinking.1: Choose a standard for judging and test with that standard
y-m-02-01.thinking.2: Make and explain, in words, an example of another shape that fits the standard
y-m-02-01.prereq.0: You can recognize triangle, quadrilateral, and circle shapes and say their names.
y-m-02-01.prereq.1: You can count 'straight lines' and 'pointed corners' by pointing at them with a finger. (Counting numbers up to 4)
y-m-02-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick the one line in Harin's thinking that is hard to trust. (Two lines may be hard to trust.)
y-m-02-01.s.s1.hint.0: For the three cards, point with your finger and count how many straight lines and how many pointed corners there are.
y-m-02-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, separate whether the reason Harin gave is something 'counted' or a 'feeling from how it looks'.
y-m-02-01.s.s1.line.0: Card 가 has four straight lines and four pointed corners, so it is a quadrilateral.
y-m-02-01.s.s1.line.1: Card 나 is long sideways, so it is not a quadrilateral.
y-m-02-01.s.s1.line.2: Card 다 is tilted, but it has four straight lines and four pointed corners.
y-m-02-01.s.s1.line.3: So a quadrilateral must have all four straight lines the same length.
y-m-02-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 4 are hard to trust. Lines 1 and 3 were said by counting straight lines and pointed corners. Line 2 was decided only by looking at 'it is long', and line 4 stretched what was seen in card 가 alone into 'they must all be the same length'. Even if it is long or tilted, the four straight lines and four pointed corners stay the same.
y-m-02-01.s.s2.prompt: When deciding whether card 나 is a quadrilateral or not, what is the most reliable thing to look at?
y-m-02-01.s.s2.hint.1: Say what is the same and what is different among cards 가, 나, and 다.
y-m-02-01.s.s2.o.a: See whether it is the same size as the first quadrilateral card you saw
y-m-02-01.s.s2.r.a: Size is not a clue for deciding the name of a shape. A big quadrilateral and a small quadrilateral are both quadrilaterals.
y-m-02-01.s.s2.o.b: See whether the direction the card is placed is correct
y-m-02-01.s.s2.r.b: The shape stays the same even if you turn it. The direction it is placed has nothing to do with the name of the shape.
y-m-02-01.s.s2.explain: How many straight lines and how many pointed corners there are are clues that do not change even if you make the shape bigger or turn it. Size, the direction it is placed, and whether the lengths are the same cannot be used as the standard for deciding the name of a shape.
y-m-02-01.s.s3.prompt: Write what you would say to Harin. Describe in words one card that looks different from 가 but is still a quadrilateral (for example, how long it is, how it is placed), and write the reason why it can be called a quadrilateral.
y-m-02-01.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine stretching card 가 out very long or laying it on its side.
y-m-02-01.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many straight lines and pointed corners that card has too, and put those numbers in your reason.
y-m-02-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear how the card you described in words is different from 가?
y-m-02-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give, as a reason, how many straight lines and pointed corners that card has?
y-m-02-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about why 'the lengths must be the same' is not needed?
y-m-02-01.s.s3.model.0: Harin, a very long card is a quadrilateral too. It has four straight lines and four pointed corners. Even if it is long, that stays the same.
y-m-02-01.s.s3.model.1: A card that is 가 laid on its side or tilted is also a quadrilateral. Even if you turn it, there are still 4 straight lines and 4 pointed corners.
y-m-02-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An example that changes the direction it is placed without making a new shape. This is also valid.

y-m-02-02.title: Is bigger heavier? Lifting it and weighing it
y-m-02-02.goal: See when the idea 'bigger is heavier' is right and when it is not, keep adjusting your judgment each time new information comes up, and make a pair that is similar in size but seems different in weight.
y-m-02-02.material: Jiho said, "Bigger is heavier." The teacher said let's test Jiho's words. She shows two objects at a time, you lift them in both hands, and at the end you check by putting them on a balance scale. (On a balance scale, the heavier side goes down.)
y-m-02-02.thinking.0: Decide whether to change or keep your judgment with new information
y-m-02-02.thinking.1: Separate the cases where it is right from the cases where it is not
y-m-02-02.thinking.2: Decide on a way to check yourself
y-m-02-02.prereq.0: The experience of lifting two objects in both hands and saying heavy/light
y-m-02-02.prereq.1: Knowing that on a balance scale (seesaw), the side that goes down is heavier.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.prompt: Each time a new piece of information comes up, think about which side will be heavier. When new information comes up, it is fine to keep your thought or to change it.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.hint.0: Look at each piece of information and first say one thing that is the same and one thing that is different from the last pair.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.hint.1: Say what point in this information your chosen answer is based on.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.info: First pair: two stones of the same kind. One is as big as a fist and one is as small as a chestnut.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which side do you think will be heavier?
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.after: If they are the same kind of stone, it is fine both to guess that the big stone is heavier and to say you will decide after lifting them. In this pair, 'bigger is heavier' fits well.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This used the idea that when it is the same kind, the bigger one has more material in it.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: There is not yet a clue to think the small one is heavier. Recall what clue made you think so.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It's hard to decide before lifting them
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a careful idea that wants to check first. Also think about how many clues there are.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.info: When lifted in both hands, the hand holding the big stone went further down. The second pair is a different kind. One is a sponge ball as big as two palms (it sinks right in when you press it), and one is a steel marble as small as a thumbnail.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: This time, which side do you think will be heavier?
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Just because the first pair was right, you cannot use the same idea for this pair. This is because the material is different. Both the guess that the steel marble seems heavier and the statement that it is hard to decide from size alone are suitable.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The big sponge ball is heavier
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You carried over the idea that was right in the first pair as it is. For this pair, first check whether the material is the same.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The small steel marble is heavier
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You used the difference in material (a sponge that can be pressed and hard steel) as a clue.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The material is different, so it's hard to decide from size alone
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You saw that a clue other than size is needed. Also think about what to do to check.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.info: When put on the balance scale, the side with the small steel marble went down. The side with the big sponge ball went up.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would be a good way to fix Jiho's words "Bigger is heavier"?
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.after: It helps between objects of the same kind, but when the kinds are different, size alone cannot decide weight. So 'always' is too strong, and even if you guess by size, it is more reliable to check by lifting it or using a scale.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It's not always so. When it was the same kind, the bigger one was heavier, but when the kinds are different it's different.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: I split it into the two stones and the two pairs of sponge and steel marble and said it.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Size doesn't matter at all. The smaller one is heavier.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You stretched the result of one pair to cover every case. Recall again how the stones in the first pair were.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Jiho is right. The sponge ball is bigger, so the scale is wrong.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: When the expectation and the result were different, you doubted the result. Look once more at what you checked with the scale.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Don't decide by size; you have to check by lifting it or putting it on a scale.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You chose the method of checking directly rather than going by size.
y-m-02-02.s.s1.reflect: In the first pair, the idea 'the big stone is heavier' was a judgment that could be kept, and in the second pair, new information that the material changes meant that idea could no longer be used as it was. The key of this activity is to say up to which pieces of information your idea is right by adding conditions.
y-m-02-02.s.s2.prompt: Write one pair of two objects that look similar in size but seem to be quite different in weight. And write how you would check it.
y-m-02-02.s.s2.hint.0: Think of two objects in your classroom or home and compare their sizes first.
y-m-02-02.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what you would feel if you held those two objects one in each hand, and which side would go down if you put them on a scale.
y-m-02-02.s.s2.placeholder: Example: ... and ... are similar in size, but ...
y-m-02-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the two objects you chose really similar in size?
y-m-02-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you decide which of the two objects you think is heavier?
y-m-02-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you actually compare the weight with the method you wrote?
y-m-02-02.s.s2.model.0: A ball of cotton and a pebble are similar in size, but I think the pebble is heavier. I would check by holding one in each hand or putting them on a balance scale.
y-m-02-02.s.s2.model.1: An empty box and a box with books in it are the same size, but the box with books is heavier. If I put them on a seesaw, I can tell which side goes down.
y-m-02-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: An example where what is inside one object is different is also valid.

y-m-02-03.title: A book that is third from the left, which place is it from the right?
y-m-02-03.topic: Position and order: saying position according to a reference
y-m-02-03.goal: Say the same spot by the number counted from the left and the number counted from the right, find the pattern between the two numbers, make several possible spots, and find out cases where information is missing.
y-m-02-03.material: 7 books are standing in a row on one shelf of a bookcase. Left and right are the left and right as seen standing in front of the bookcase. The books are in a continuous row with no gaps. Mina counted the blue book from the left and said 'second', and Seohyeon counted from the right and said 'sixth'. Both of them counted correctly.
y-m-02-03.thinking.0: Knowing that when the reference changes, the words for calling the same thing change too
y-m-02-03.thinking.1: Make several spots that fit a condition
y-m-02-03.thinking.2: Judge whether the information is enough
y-m-02-03.prereq.1: Words that show order such as first, second, and third
y-m-02-03.s.s1.prompt: Could the books Mina and Seohyeon spoke of be the same book?
y-m-02-03.s.s1.hint.0: Draw the 7 books as 7 circles and write the numbers 1, 2, 3, ... from the left.
y-m-02-03.s.s1.hint.1: In the same circles, also write the numbers counted from the right and find the spot that is second.
y-m-02-03.s.s1.o.a: They are different books. Second and sixth are different spots
y-m-02-03.s.s1.r.a: You thought that different counted numbers mean different spots. Did you think about which side the row is counted from?
y-m-02-03.s.s1.o.b: They could be the same book. They counted from opposite sides
y-m-02-03.s.s1.r.b: This idea is that if the side you count from is different, the same book can get a different number.
y-m-02-03.s.s1.o.c: You can't tell. Because you don't know how many books there are
y-m-02-03.s.s1.r.c: You missed the information that there are 7 books. Look at whether the needed information is already there in this situation.
y-m-02-03.s.s1.explain: If a row has 7 books, there are 5 books to the right of the second book from the left. Seen from the right, that book has 5 books in front of it, so it is sixth. The numbers are different only because the side counted from is different; it is the same book.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.prompt: A red book is on the same bookshelf (7 books). Make 2 different spots so that the red book is to the left of the middle (fourth). Write in a the place from the left and in b the place from the right. The two numbers must point to the same one book.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.hint.0: Start by writing the number counted from the left and the number counted from the right together on a row of 7 circles.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.hint.1: First count how many spots there are to the left of the middle (fourth).
y-m-02-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The number counted from the left is a number from 1 to 7.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number counted from the left must be a natural number from 1 to 7.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The number counted from the right is a number from 1 to 7.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The number counted from the right must be a natural number from 1 to 7.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The two numbers point to the same one book.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.fail.c3: These two numbers do not point to the same book. Write the numbers on a row of 7 books and check.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.ok.c4: It is to the left of the middle (fourth).
y-m-02-03.s.s2.fail.c4: It is not to the left of the middle (fourth).
y-m-02-03.s.s2.explain: The possible spots are three: (1,7), (2,6), and (3,5). The fourth spot is fourth from the left and also fourth from the right, so it is not 'to the left of the middle'.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Write, using numbers, how b is decided once a is decided, that is, the pattern you found between the two numbers.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the two numbers of the two spots you made side by side and compare how they are related to each other.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Look at what happens to the right number when the left number goes up by one.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If it is ...th from the left, it is ...th from the right.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the pattern you wrote right in both or more of the spots you made?
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that the pattern is used only when there are 7 books?
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If it is 3rd from the left, it is 5th from the right. When you add the two numbers, it is always 8.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.model.1: Each time the left number goes up by 1, the right number goes down by 1. Like 1st and 7th, 2nd and 6th.
y-m-02-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It was said by how it changes without using the sum. This is also valid.
y-m-02-03.s.s3.prompt: On another bookcase, you do not know how many books there are. You were only told that the green book is third from the left. Can you say which place this book is from the right?
y-m-02-03.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine putting one more book at the right end and look at whether the order of the green book from the left changes.
y-m-02-03.s.s3.hint.1: Draw the case of 5 books and the case of 7 books and compare which place it is from the right.
y-m-02-03.s.s3.o.d: Whatever the number of books, which place it is from the right is fixed
y-m-02-03.s.s3.r.d: You thought the number stays the same even if books increase. Think about what happens if you put one more book on the right.
y-m-02-03.s.s3.explain: Knowing only that it is third from the left, you cannot tell how many books are to its right. If there are 5 books, it is third from the right, and if there are 7 books, it is fifth from the right. You can decide only when you know how many books there are in all.

y-m-02-04.title: Does a tall cup hold more water?
y-m-02-04.goal: Choose reliable ways to test the idea 'if it is tall, it holds more', judge by the result of pouring from one to the other, and make in words the shape of cups for which that idea is wrong.
y-m-02-04.material: Cup 가 is a very tall, narrow cup. Cup 나 is a short, very wide cup. Both cups are open at the top and smooth inside. Ain said, "가 is taller, so 가 holds more water." Junho said, "Let's not go by what we see, let's check with water."
y-m-02-04.thinking.1: Judge by the result of an experiment
y-m-02-04.thinking.2: Make a shape that is a counterexample
y-m-02-04.prereq.0: The experience of filling a cup full of water
y-m-02-04.prereq.1: Comparing in words as 'more / less / the same'
y-m-02-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the ways to find out reliably which cup holds more water.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.hint.1: Separate whether each method directly compares 'the amount of water it holds' or compares something else (height, weight of the cup).
y-m-02-04.s.s1.o.a: Put the two cups side by side and look only at the height
y-m-02-04.s.s1.r.a: Height is only one clue. You cannot tell how wide the cup is.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.o.b: Pour the water filled to the top of cup 가 into cup 나 and look
y-m-02-04.s.s1.r.b: This is a method of pouring water directly to compare the sizes of the two cups. Also think about how to read the result.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.o.c: Lift them in your hands and pick the heavier cup
y-m-02-04.s.s1.r.c: You would be weighing the cup itself. Think about whether that is the same as the amount of water it holds.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.o.d: Count how many times you fill it with the same small container
y-m-02-04.s.s1.r.d: This is a method that uses the same container as a unit and compares the two cups with the same standard.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.explain: If you pour water directly or count the number of times you fill them with the same container, you can compare the amount of water the cups hold, no matter the shape of the cups. Looking only at height or lifting empty cups does not directly compare the amount of water they hold.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.acc.0: Pouring alone can give a reliable result. It is good to also know that there is a method of counting with the same container.
y-m-02-04.s.s1.acc.1: The method of counting times with the same small container is also reliable. It is good to also know that there is a method of pouring.
y-m-02-04.s.s2.prompt: Junho filled cup 가 with water and poured it all into cup 나 without spilling a drop, and the water in cup 나 filled only about halfway up the cup. What can be said from this result?
y-m-02-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write in words both that the water in cup 가 was a full amount and that cup 나 was not filled by that water.
y-m-02-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether more water from cup 가 would be needed to fill cup 나.
y-m-02-04.s.s2.r.a: You read that the poured water did not fill the cup, and compared the sizes of the two cups.
y-m-02-04.s.s2.r.b: You put the first thought that it is tall ahead of the result. Think about what it means that all the water of 가 was moved and 나 is not full.
y-m-02-04.s.s2.o.c: The two cups hold the same amount of water
y-m-02-04.s.s2.r.c: Look at whether the water that filled the cup filled cup 나.
y-m-02-04.s.s2.o.d: Don't judge before trying one more time
y-m-02-04.s.s2.explain: The water that filled cup 가 filled only about half of cup 나, so cup 나 can hold more water than that. The first idea (if it is tall, it holds more) was not right for this pair of cups.
y-m-02-04.s.s3.prompt: Describe in words two cups for which Ain's "if it is tall, it holds more water" may not be right. Write the height and width (narrow or wide) of the two cups, and also write which cup holds more water.
y-m-02-04.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine filling both cups with water to the same height and compare which side holds more water.
y-m-02-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: One cup is ... and the other cup is ...
y-m-02-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the two cups you described, is it clear which is taller and which is wider?
y-m-02-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did it turn out to be a shape where the short cup, not the tall cup, holds more water?
y-m-02-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Could you check whether my words are right by pouring or by counting with the same container?
y-m-02-04.s.s3.model.0: Let's say the tall cup is very thin, and the short cup is very wide. The short, wide cup can hold more water.
y-m-02-04.s.s3.model.1: One cup is tall but narrow, and the other is a little shorter but much thicker. The thick cup can hold more. You can tell by pouring the water of the tall cup into it.
y-m-02-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that also adds a way to check.

y-m-02-05.title: If the ending mark is greater, is it longer?
y-m-02-05.goal: Understand that information about only one end is not enough to compare lengths, say that you also need to know where each starts, fix your first judgment with new information, and choose a way to compare directly.
y-m-02-05.material: On a desk, pencil 가 and pencil 나 lie straight side by side next to a ruler. The ruler has marks from 0 to 10, and the gaps between the marks are all equal. All you can see right now is the right ends. The right end of pencil 가 is at mark 9, and the right end of pencil 나 is at mark 8. You have not yet seen the left ends of the two pencils. Eunseo said, "가's end reaches mark 9, so 가 is longer."
y-m-02-05.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
y-m-02-05.thinking.1: Fix your judgment with new information
y-m-02-05.prereq.0: The meaning of 0 on a ruler and one space between marks
y-m-02-05.prereq.1: Comparing length in words as 'longer / shorter / the same'
y-m-02-05.s.s1.prompt: What else do you need to know to decide whether Eunseo's words are right?
y-m-02-05.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine one pencil lying on the ruler, and say at how many marks you need to know its position to know its length.
y-m-02-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the length differs when the left end of a pencil whose right end is at 9 is at 0 and when it is at 7.
y-m-02-05.s.s1.o.a: Whether the two pencils are equally thick
y-m-02-05.s.s1.r.a: Thickness is not information used to compare length. Length is decided by from where to where.
y-m-02-05.s.s1.o.b: How many spaces are left to the end of the ruler (mark 10)
y-m-02-05.s.s1.r.b: You already know the mark of the right end, so this repeats the same information. Look at whether it tells you anything new.
y-m-02-05.s.s1.o.c: At which mark the left end of each of the two pencils is
y-m-02-05.s.s1.r.c: You saw that you need both where the pencil starts and where it ends.
y-m-02-05.s.s1.o.d: Which of the two pencils is sharpened to a sharper point
y-m-02-05.s.s1.r.d: You need to look at where the pencil is placed, not how it is sharpened. Think about what information is needed when reading length from marks.
y-m-02-05.s.s1.explain: Length is from the place the pencil starts to the place it ends. The mark of the right end alone cannot decide which pencil is longer; you need to know at which mark the left end is.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.prompt: Now the left ends are known. 가 starts at mark 5 and 나 starts at mark 0. Seohyeon thought it over again with this information. Pick the line in Seohyeon's words that is hard to trust.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.hint.0: Point with your finger at the marks from which to which 가 and 나 each lie, and count the spaces.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the pencil with the greater ending mark also started from the same place.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.line.0: 가 lies from mark 5 to mark 9.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.line.1: 나 lies from mark 0 to mark 8.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.line.2: 가, whose ending mark is greater, is longer.
y-m-02-05.s.s2.explain: Lines 3 and 4 are hard to trust. Lines 1 and 2 read the marks accurately. 가 goes from mark 5 to 9, so it is 4 spaces, and 나 goes from mark 0 to 8, so it is 8 spaces. Line 3, which compared only the ending marks, ignored the place where they start, so the conclusion of line 4 cannot be trusted either. With the newly learned information, Eunseo's first judgment has to be fixed.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.prompt: Even without a ruler, how can you place two pencils to compare their lengths reliably? Choose all the suitable ways.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine what changes if you place the two pencils side by side with one end against the corner of the desk.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.hint.1: When one end is on the same line, say where on the remaining end you should look to compare the lengths.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.o.a: Line up the left ends of the two pencils on the same line and look at the right ends
y-m-02-05.s.s3.r.a: This idea is that once you line up one end, you only need to compare the position of the remaining end.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.o.b: Line up the right ends of the two pencils on the same line and look at the left ends
y-m-02-05.s.s3.r.b: This idea is that you can line up either end.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.o.c: Put the two pencils far apart from each other and look with your eyes
y-m-02-05.s.s3.r.c: Seen from far away, they look different depending on where they are placed and your eye level. Think about whether that is the same as putting them against each other to compare.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.o.d: Say the pencil whose right end sticks out further is longer, just like that
y-m-02-05.s.s3.r.d: You carried over, just as it was, the mistake of looking only at the right end seen in the ruler problem.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.explain: If you line up one end on the same line, the pencil whose remaining end sticks out further is longer. It does not matter which end you line up. Putting them far apart or looking at only one end is not a reliable comparison.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.acc.0: The method of lining up the left ends is reliable. It is good to also know that lining up the right ends makes the same comparison.
y-m-02-05.s.s3.acc.1: The method of lining up the right ends is also reliable. It is good to also know that lining up the left ends makes the same comparison.

y-m-02-06.title: Decorating a poster with 8 pieces: what ways are possible?
y-m-02-06.topic: Plane figures: decorating with shape pieces
y-m-02-06.goal: Make not one but several combinations of numbers of shape pieces that keep several conditions at once, and compare ways of finding them without missing any.
y-m-02-06.material: Saerom's class decorates a poster with triangle, quadrilateral, and circle shaped pieces. In all, 8 pieces must be stuck on. There are three conditions. ① Use at least one each of triangle, quadrilateral, and circle pieces. ② Use fewer quadrilateral pieces than triangle pieces. ③ There are 8 pieces in all. (There is no picture, so think only about the number of pieces.)
y-m-02-06.thinking.0: Keeping several conditions at the same time
y-m-02-06.thinking.1: Finding different solutions under the same conditions
y-m-02-06.thinking.2: Evaluating ways of finding without missing any
y-m-02-06.prereq.0: Knowing triangle, quadrilateral, and circle shapes
y-m-02-06.prereq.1: Counting numbers up to 10 and comparing 'more / fewer'
y-m-02-06.prereq.2: Pairing up numbers up to 10 (for example, pairs that split 8 into two)
y-m-02-06.s.s1.prompt: Four friends decided the numbers of pieces. Pick the plans that do not keep the conditions. (There may be two or more.)
y-m-02-06.s.s1.hint.0: Check the three conditions one at a time for each plan. First count all the pieces and see whether there are 8.
y-m-02-06.s.s1.hint.1: Then put the numbers of quadrilateral pieces and triangle pieces side by side and compare which is fewer.
y-m-02-06.s.s1.explain: Line 2 (Haeun) and line 4 (Seoa) did not keep the conditions. Haeun has 8 pieces, but the quadrilateral pieces are not fewer than the triangle pieces (2 and 2). Seoa has fewer quadrilateral pieces than triangle pieces, but all the pieces put together make 9. Lines 1 and 3 keep all three conditions.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different ways of numbers of pieces that keep all three conditions. Write it as a triangles, b quadrilaterals, and c circles.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.hint.0: Decide that there is 1 quadrilateral piece and think about the numbers of the other pieces.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.hint.1: First decide how many triangles and circles together there must be, then check whether there are more triangles than quadrilaterals.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All the numbers of pieces are natural numbers.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of pieces must be numbers you can count and say, like 0, 1, 2, ....
y-m-02-06.s.s2.ok.c2: You used at least one of all three shapes.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.fail.c2: You must use at least one each of triangle, quadrilateral, and circle.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.ok.c3: There are fewer quadrilateral pieces than triangle pieces.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.fail.c3: There are not fewer quadrilateral pieces than triangle pieces.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.fail.c4: There are not 8 pieces in all. Count all three numbers.
y-m-02-06.s.s2.explain: There are 9 pairs of numbers of pieces in all that keep the conditions. Finding just one is fine, but it is important to check that there are several different pairs.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.prompt: How can you find all the possible pairs of numbers of pieces without missing any? Choose all the suitable ways.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.hint.0: Organize the pairs you found in a table, and split them so that one row is 1 quadrilateral, the next row is 2 quadrilaterals, and so on.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.hint.1: When there is 1 quadrilateral piece, check one by one from how many to how many triangles are possible.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.o.a: Look for them as they come to mind and stop when nothing more comes to mind
y-m-02-06.s.s3.r.a: There is no way to check whether something was missed. Think about how you can know that the pairs you found are all of them.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.o.b: Fix the number of quadrilateral pieces one at a time and split up the rest
y-m-02-06.s.s3.r.b: This is a method of fixing one thing and changing the rest in order.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.o.c: Find only one way that uses the most triangles
y-m-02-06.s.s3.r.c: You thought you are done once you find one example. This activity is about looking at whether there are several possible ones.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.o.d: Fix the number of circle pieces one at a time and split up the rest
y-m-02-06.s.s3.r.d: This is a method of fixing a different one and changing the rest in order. Think about whether you can find them all with no gaps whichever shape you fix.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.explain: If you fix the number of one shape and change the rest one at a time, you can tell how far you have searched, so you can find them without missing any. If you look as things come to mind or stop at one, you cannot tell whether a pair was missed.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.acc.0: The method of fixing the number of quadrilateral pieces is a way to find them without missing any. The method of fixing the circles is the same way.
y-m-02-06.s.s3.acc.1: The method of fixing the number of circle pieces is also a way to find them without missing any. The method of fixing the quadrilaterals is the same way.
